content.rendered:
PDFs are where sensitive documents live — contracts, invoices, IDs, medical results. That is exactly why these free PDF tools run entirely in your browser: the file is opened, edited and converted on your own device, and nothing is ever uploaded. No signup, no page limits, no watermarks — just open a tool and work.

Edit, sign and whiteout with the PDF Editor

The PDF Editor is the flagship of this category. Open any PDF and you can add text in matching fonts, draw or type a signature, whiteout anything that should not be there, drop in images, delete or reorder pages, zoom in for precision, and export a standard PDF that opens everywhere. It covers the everyday cases that normally push people into paid subscriptions: filling a form that arrived flat, signing a lease, redacting an account number before forwarding a statement.

Convert PDF pages to images

Sometimes you don’t need a PDF — you need a picture of it: for a slide, a web page, a WhatsApp message, or a system that only accepts images. Five converters render each page at print-quality resolution and download the results, one image per page:

  • PDF to JPG — the universal choice; smallest files, opens anywhere.
  • PDF to PNG — lossless and crisp; the right pick for text-heavy pages and screenshots.
  • PDF to WebP — modern web format; sharp pages at noticeably smaller sizes for your own site.
  • PDF to TIFF — the archival/print standard many scanners, fax gateways and legal workflows require.
  • PDF to AVIF — the newest format, with the best compression of all for web publishing.

Which conversion should you pick?

Use JPG when the page is going to email, chat or an upload form. Use PNG when small text must stay razor sharp. Use WebP or AVIF when you control the website and care about load speed. Use TIFF only when a workflow explicitly demands it — the files are large by design.

Worked example: signing and returning a contract

A contract arrives by email with “please sign and return.” Open it in the PDF Editor, click the signature tool, draw your signature once, place it on the line, add today’s date as text, and export. If the sender then asks for “page 3 as an image for our records,” run the signed file through PDF to JPG and send page 3. The contract never touched a third-party server at any step.

Why your PDFs should never touch a server

Think about the last five PDFs you handled: a contract, a payslip, an ID scan, a medical result, an invoice. Uploading those to a free converter site means trusting an unknown company’s storage, retention and breach record with your most sensitive documents. The tools here make that trust unnecessary: PDF parsing and rendering run inside your browser using the same open-source engine (PDF.js lineage) browsers themselves use, and exports are assembled locally. Close the tab and no copy exists anywhere but your device. For anything involving signatures, finances or identity, client-side is not a nice-to-have — it is the only architecture that should be acceptable.

Common PDF jobs, mapped to the right tool

“Fill and sign this form” — the PDF Editor‘s text and signature tools. “Hide the account number before forwarding” — the editor’s whiteout, exported as flattened vector so nothing peeks through. “Drop pages 4–7” — the editor’s page delete. “Put page 1 in a PowerPoint slide” — PDF to PNG for crisp text. “The portal only accepts images” — PDF to JPG. “Legal wants TIFF for archiving” — PDF to TIFF. “Publish the brochure pages on our site, fast” — PDF to WebP or PDF to AVIF for the smallest sharp files.

Going the other direction? The image tools compress and convert the pictures you just exported, and the full tools index lists everything on the site.
